title: I Took the Gelato-Batch Freezer Booking to the Chef Who Left My Numbered Paddles

parts.text: I stepped into the batch bay at 8:06 a.m. and chef Lia was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE FREEZER. FORTY MINUTES. PADDLES STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was twenty-nine, kitchen secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered paddles. Lia shrugged. "Chefs are the batch." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover mix on my numbered paddles. Then I asked for the batch log. At 8:14 the bay pinged why Lia's name was on my mix. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The bay can see Lia's leftover mix on my numbered paddles.

social.video_title: She left my numbered gelato paddles on my freezer — Part 1/2
social.description: Batch bay, leftover mix, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the paddles. Would you have asked for the batch log?

parts.text: Lia called it overrun until the bay asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the mix still. The paddles went back to my numbered booking. Lia ran a slot of her own and told the next chef atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CHEFS ARE NOT THE BATCH. I keep my paddles on a labeled rack. Lia brown-bags her overrun. The bay finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chefs are not the batch — Part 2/2
social.description: Batch log, numbered paddles, and a second line on the board. Was overrun ever my mix?
